evidence.quote: Guidelines on when to screen for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia apply to infants born at 35 weeks or later of gestation.
There is a need to develop guidelines to optimize hyperbilirubinemia screening among early preterm infants.
The rates of newborns requiring phototherapy were 52% in the first 3 days, 16% from the 4th to the 7th day, and 2% during the second week.
Among very preterm babies, TcB measurements might be useful for screening for neonatal jaundice in the first 2 weeks of life.
Bilirubin was measured at least once daily for the first 7 days after birth for all infants.
TcB measurements were obtained using the BiliCheck bilirubinometer (SpectRx Inc., Norcross, Georgia, USA) as part of routine clinical care.

Measurements were obtained every 12–24 h during the first week of life, with additional measurements performed when clinically indicated or when bilirubin concentrations approached treatment thresholds.

claims.summary: A TcB at least 3 mg/dL below the phototherapy cutpoint gave a ≥98% probability that TSB was below that cutpoint in a sample starting at 26 0/7 weeks PMA, with a conclusion that covers 28-34 6/7 weeks [Maisels2015], the corrected Table 4 of cutpoints by PMA starts at 28 0/7 weeks with no row below 28 weeks [Maisels2015Erratum], and the high-risk phototherapy value of 5 mg/dL for <28 weeks is known here only second-hand, from Table 1 of the Stavis preprint [Stavis2026]; sources differ on TcB at this age, since a California multicenter study supports TcB screening below 30 weeks [Sankar2023], a California NICU survey made no recommendation below 28 weeks [Bhatt2018] and NICE uses serum bilirubin below 35 weeks [NICE2023]; no retrieved source sets a notification level.

evidence.quote: Nursing staff performed 896 TcB measurements within 1 h of a TSB on 225 neonates 26 0/7-34 6/7 weeks' postmenstrual age (PMA).

Our data support the use of routine TcB screening for infants 28-34 6/7 weeks' gestation.

claims.summary: For infants ≥35 weeks the 2022 AAP guideline replaced the Bhutani-based nomogram with the difference between bilirubin and the phototherapy threshold and measures TSB when TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of that threshold or is ≥15 mg/dL [Kemper2022], the Canadian Paediatric Society statement for ≥35 weeks proposes that difference in place of the predictive nomogram and confirms with TSB when TcB is within 50 µmol/L of the phototherapy threshold or above 250 µmol/L (calculated about 2.9 and 14.6 mg/dL) [CPS2026], BiliTool states that there are no more risk zones [BiliTool2026], the nomogram came from direct Coombs negative healthy term and near-term newborns [Bhutani1999], NICE checks a transcutaneous reading above 250 micromol/litre with serum bilirubin [NICE2023], and no retrieved source keeps a fixed value of 13 mg/dL.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests that the 2022 AAP guideline no longer uses the Bhutani-based risk nomogram, which did not account for gestational age or neurotoxicity risk factors and excluded DAT-positive infants [Kemper2022]. For infants ≥35 weeks, it recommends TSB when TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy threshold or is ≥15 mg/dL, and bases further testing on the difference between bilirubin and that threshold [Kemper2022]. The Canadian statement also proposes that difference, with TSB if TcB is within 50 µmol/L of the threshold or above 250 µmol/L [CPS2026].

evidence.quote: TSB should be measured if the TcB exceeds or is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy treatment threshold or if the TcB is ≥15 mg/dL.

Those follow-up recommendations used a previous risk nomogram (Fig 2 in the 2004 guideline, based on the 1999 study of Bhutani et al) that did not take gestational age and hyperbilirubinemia neurotoxicity risk factors into account and was created from a study population that excluded DAT positive infants.

The current guideline recommends using the difference between the bilirubin concentration and the phototherapy threshold at the time of measurement to determine the interval between discharge and follow-up and the need for additional TSB or TcB measurements (Fig 7).

When TcB testing is used to monitor infants with hyperbilirubinemia, obtain confirmatory testing with TSB if the TcB level is within 50 µmol/L of the hour-specific phototherapy threshold OR if the TcB is above 250 µmol/L.

evidence.quote: For infants in the aggressive-phototherapy group, phototherapy was initiated at enrollment (when the bilirubin level was expected to be approximately 5 mg per deciliter).

Aggressive phototherapy, as compared with conservative phototherapy, significantly reduced the mean peak serum bilirubin level (7.0 vs. 9.8 mg per deciliter [120 vs. 168 μmol per liter], P<0.01) but not the rate of the primary outcome (52% vs. 55%; relative risk, 0.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.87 to 1.02; P = 0.15).
Aggressive phototherapy did not significantly reduce the rate of death or neurodevelopmental impairment.

The rate of neurodevelopmental impairment alone was significantly reduced with aggressive phototherapy. This reduction may be offset by an increase in mortality among infants weighing 501 to 750 g at birth.

claims.manual_text: IVIG for ABO and Rh incompatibility: Dose: 1g/kg/dose
claims.summary: The AAP gives 0.5 to 1 g/kg for infants ≥35 weeks [Kemper2022], the Canadian Paediatric Society gives the same range for infants ≥35 weeks if an exchange transfusion cannot be readily performed and advises against routine use [CPS2026], NICE gives 500 mg/kg [NICE2023], and an international panel gives no dose, does not recommend routine, prophylactic IVIG before exchange level, and calls its role unclear when exchange transfusion is imminent or not readily available [Lieberman2022]; a randomized trial in Rh disease found 0.5 and 1 g/kg similar but was not powered for exchange transfusion, IVIg did not reduce exchange transfusions in the subgroup born at less than 37 weeks [Zwiers2018], and a meta-analysis found fewer exchange transfusions but possibly no additional clinical benefit [Roberts2026].

These recommendations conclude that IVIG should not be routinely used to treat Rh or ABO antibody‐mediated HDN.

evidence.quote: Term and preterm infants with Rh or ABO (or both) incompatibility were included.

The only randomized controlled trial comparing the effect of two doses of IVIg in Rh HDN showed that 0.5 g/kg and 1 g/kg had a similar effect on the duration of phototherapy, duration of hospitalization and ET requirements (Girish 2008). However, this study was not powered to detect a difference in the need for ET.

evidence.quote: the two studies at lowest risk of bias show no benefit of IVIg in reducing the need for and number of exchange transfusions.
In the subgroup of infants born at less than 37 weeks of gestation, IVIg did not reduce the use of ETs (82 participants, typical RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.91; NNTB 20) (data not shown)
Eligible studies included randomised controlled trials and observational cohorts evaluating IVIG in HDN.
Subgroup analysis suggested that the reduction in ET was more consistent in Rh-mediated HDN (OR = 0.2; CI: 0.1-0.8; I2 = 81%) than in ABO-mediated HDN (OR = 0.76; CI: 0.1-4.1; I2 = 89%).
Despite reducing ET requirements, adjunctive IVIG with phototherapy may not provide additional clinical benefits compared with phototherapy alone.
